cards.back: Under 1 ms p50 and 3 ms p99. The limiter must cost less than the requests it protects.

cards.front: Counter operations at 1M requests a second
cards.back: About 2.5M a second, since each request checks about 2.5 limits (key, user or IP, sometimes endpoint).
About 3 GB (2.5 buckets each at about 100 bytes). It fits in memory several times over.
As a library inside each API gateway (or a sidecar), not a separate network hop.
429 Too Many Requests with Retry-After and RateLimit-* headers. Send the RateLimit headers on every response so clients slow down early.

cards.front: Why a Lua script in Redis?
cards.back: GET then SET from the gateway races; INCR can't express refill. A script runs the read-modify-write as one atomic step on the shard.

cards.front: Token bucket vs daily quota counter
cards.back: Token bucket for rates (bursts up to bucket size, steady refill); a plain counter with a TTL for daily quotas.
All of one key's buckets land on one shard, so one script checks them together and refuses all if any refuses.
A gateway takes a small batch of tokens from Redis and spends them from memory, cutting round trips. Worst-case overshoot is gateways × lease size.
Once a key is refused, the gateway remembers until its reset time, so an abusive client gets 429s from memory without touching Redis.
Fail open (with local limits) for a public API; fail closed for limits guarding money or security, like logins, password resets and SMS sends.

cards.front: Why not one global Redis across regions?
cards.back: It would add 70-150 ms to every request. Each region keeps its own counters, with a static split or async usage sync.

quiz.q: Two gateways both see one token left for a key and both allow the request. What is the root cause?
choices: The read-modify-write isn't atomic; it should be one Lua script in Redis
quiz.why: A separate GET and SET leaves a race; the script runs as one step.

quiz.q: A customer with a limit of 10 requests a minute regularly gets 40 through. Leases are 20 tokens across 300 gateways. What is the fix?
choices: Send small limits straight to Redis on every check and scale leases with the limit
Move the limiter to a separate service
quiz.why: Overshoot is bounded by gateways × lease size, so small limits must skip leasing.

quiz.q: A Redis shard fails over and p99 jumps above 5 ms. What should gateways do for the public API?
choices: Reject every request until Redis recovers
Trip a circuit breaker and enforce limit ÷ gateways from local memory
Route checks to another region's Redis
quiz.why: Failing open with approximate local limits keeps the API up while still capping abuse.

quiz.q: The limiter guards SMS verification sends, and Redis is down. What is the right behaviour?
choices: Use the static split from last week
quiz.why: Limits guarding money or security should fail closed.

quiz.q: An abusive client sends 50,000 requests a second after being limited and Redis CPU climbs. What helps most?
choices: A local deny cache that answers 429 from memory until reset
quiz.why: Refusals cached locally never touch Redis.

quiz.q: One enterprise customer makes a single Redis shard run hot. What do you do?
choices: Split their bucket into N sub-buckets on different shards, each with 1/N of the rate
Turn off hash tags for everyone
quiz.why: Sub-buckets spread one hot key across shards.

quiz.q: Right after a config push, 429s spike for every plan. What safeguard should have caught it?
choices: Staged rule rollouts with a dry-run mode and instant rollback
quiz.why: A bad rule can block everyone, so rules roll out in stages and can log without enforcing.
